title: TB8-01749
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the "principal Appellant") and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "associate Appellant"), who are both nationals of Nepal, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the "principal Appellant") and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "associate Appellant"), who are both nationals of Nepal, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.

The Appellants have submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1 and request an oral hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. The Appellants ask that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute a decision with its own determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants request that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel.
Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellants alleged before the RPD that they are being threatened and extorted in Nepal by members of the Biplav Maoist faction in their local area. Their allegations of harm are set out in their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms.2

The Appellants' hearing for refugee protection was held on November 2, 2017. In an oral decision on the same day, the RPD rejected the Appellants' claim finding that the Appellants had an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kathmandu. The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA and in its treatment of the documentary evidence.

As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica,3 the RAD must review RPD decisions on a correctness standard with respect to questions of law and findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) which raise no issue of the credibility of oral evidence. More deference may be required when the RPD is in an advantageous position with respect to the assessment of oral evidence. ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

In support of this appeal, the Appellants submitted approximately 24 news media articles,4 as well as a series of "press releases" from the National Human Rights Commission in Nepal as proposed new evidence in this appeal.5 The RAD notes that the Appellants submit that the articles clearly contradict the assertion of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) that a viable IFA is available in Kathmandu. The Appellants submit that this evidence proves that the agents of persecution will find them in Kathmandu.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected6 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.7

The RAD finds that the three articles relating to "bomb blasts;"8 the eleven articles describing9 that the authorities have taken an active stance in protecting the public from potential violent activities associated with the efforts of the breakaway Chand CPN Maoists (Biplav); and a series of four articles10 linked to the shooting of the President of Federation of Contractors Association of Nepal (FCAN), all arose following the rejection of the Appellants' claim, hence, they meet the basic requirements of subsection 110(4). In respect to assessing the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh,11 the RAD notes the articles are credible, relevant and new. The RAD finds the articles will be admitted as new evidence in this appeal.

The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.12

The RAD notes that the Appellants provide very little explanation as to how any of the articles submitted relate to the ability of the local Biplav Maoists from their home area to locate them in the IFA location. The RAD's review of the articles relating to the December 2017 bomb blasts in the Kathmandu area confirm that the Biplav Maoists are involved in anti-election related violence, which appears to be focused towards the Nepali Congress Party. The RAD notes the principal Appellant has stated that he was a member of the Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal (National Democratic Party) in his local area. The RAD finds that none of the articles address any interaction with the National Democratic Party, nor do they provide any indication that the individuals associated with the so-called attacks were involved in extortion activities or the pursuit of other individuals.

The RAD further finds it of interest that two of the three articles13 describe that the authorities have taken an active interest in the arrest of the individuals involved and the prevention of future disruption through the pursuit and arrest of any individuals who are associated with the potential violence. The RAD finds the articles confirm that an active and fully functioning state protection mechanism is in place.

The RAD notes that seven additional articles14 confirm that the authorities have taken an active stance in protecting the public from potential violent activities associated with the efforts of the breakaway Chand CPN Maoists (Biplav) and their associates. One article states, "the law enforcement agency has already deployed special teams to identify and arrest senior leaders of the CPN, which is the only force that is objecting to the elections ... If central leaders are arrested, it would be easier to curb the violent activities launched by the Chand-led CPN." The RAD finds this further confirms the intent and actions of the government in providing state protection to all of its citizens.

The Appellants' evidence contains a series of four articles15 linked to the shooting of the President of FCAN. One of the articles titled, "Shooter among five arrested; extortion was the motive," confirms that the authorities conducted an intensive investigation, as well as generally increased the security activities in the Kathmandu valley, which led to the arrest of five gang members associated with the crime. The RAD notes that this appears to be a crime perpetrated by a gang of criminals with no linkage to the CPN Maoists. The RAD finds that as much as an individual was shot by criminals, the authorities reacted swiftly and apprehended the criminals, again demonstrating that state protection was effective.

The RAD finds that the articles submitted as new evidence indicate that Biplav Maoists do exist in Kathmandu and that they are primarily involved in terrorist type activities focused on disrupting the current election. The articles do not provide persuasive evidence that: * these individuals have any linkage to the Biplav Maoist group in their home area; * that they are involved in extortion related activities; and, * that the local Biplav group in their home area have any ability to communicate with other related groups.

As much as the Appellants have alleged that Kathmandu is not a safe location in which to reside, the Appellants own evidence confirms that there is an active and functioning state protection mechanism in place to protect them should they encounter problems.

The remaining articles16 do not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA in that they arose prior to the rejection of the Appellants' claim before the RPD. The Appellants have not provided any addition submissions as to why these documents should be admitted as new evidence. The RAD will not admit these articles as new evidence in this appeal.

The RAD has reviewed the "press releases" from the National Human Rights Commission, Nepal.17 The RAD notes the majority of the documents arose following the rejection of the Appellants' claim for refugee protection, meeting the basic requirement of subsection 110(4). The Appellants have not provided any explanation as to how these "press releases" relate to or support their allegations. The RAD notes that Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules requires that the Appellants before the RAD must file a record that includes, inter alia, the RPD's decision; all or part of the transcript of the RPD hearing; any documents the RPD refused to accept, but that the Appellants want to rely on in the appeal; as well as the Appellants' Memorandum containing full and detailed submissions regarding: (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, (ii) where the errors are located in the written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the Refugee Protection Division hearing, (iii) how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant.18

The RAD finds the Appellants' submissions accompanying the new evidence are generally vague, and that the submissions in respect of the press releases are absent. The Federal Court has stated that Appellants have the obligation to explain how the documents submitted could have affected the merits of the application.19 In particular, there are no specific references to aspects of the evidence that would support the Appellants' claims in the written submissions.20 It is insufficient to submit to a decision-maker [translation] "information in a bundle hoping that they would find a reason to agree" with an applicant.21 Rather, the Appellants have the burden of demonstrating how the RPD erred in drawing that finding with reference to the evidence, jurisprudence or rule of law. The RAD cannot be expected to comb the documentary evidence and guess why the Appellants believe the RPD erred.
The RAD will not admit these documents as new evidence in this appeal. As such, in respect to these documents, the RAD must proceed without an oral hearing.

The RPD found that the determinative issue is the availability of an IFA in Kathmandu in Nepal. The Appellants argue: 1. The RPD did not take into account the evidence on the record. 2. The RPD ignored the Appellants' explanations and the contradictory evidence. 3. The RPD finding in respect to the Appellants' testimony about how the Maoists would locate them in Kathmandu is flawed. 4. There is significant evidence that the Maoists have an extensive network throughout Nepal.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:22 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA; 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellants' identity. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellants cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.23

While an analysis of whether a particular appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA under the first prong of the Rasaratnam test is necessarily fact-specific, the RAD is aware that as a general principle, Canadian courts have held that large urban areas cannot be assumed to be an IFA by virtue of their population size alone,24 and that the distance between the proposed IFA and the location of the persecutors does not in itself serve to establish that the proposed IFA is viable.25 That said, the IFA need not be far away from where the appellant has previously lived: the concept of an IFA does not require that the safe haven be in another city or province than the place of origin so long as it is truly an area in which the appellant can seek refuge from the persecution experienced in her home district.26 Ultimately, the question of whether an appellant has shown, on a balance of probabilities, that they face a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA will turn on their evidence, keeping in mind the general principles above. First Prong

The RAD notes that the documentary evidence describes the Maoists in Nepal as a series of groups with various fragments or splinter offshoots. The documentary evidence states, "some of these groups are part of the government, while others are opposed to the government and are engaged in boycotts and violent activities [citation omitted]."27 The documentary evidence notes: "[t]here are a number of Maoist factions who have rejected accommodation with the elected government and continue political activity beyond the mainstream Maoist party," elements of which may be involved in extortion [citation omitted]."28

The evidence carries on to state: ...that instances of kidnapping and extortion by Maoist groups "are increasingly rare occurrences from a political party perspective" and are "not common any longer."... The same source indicated that "organized human rights violations/abuses are not taking place in Nepal due to the Maoist party," although there may be involvement in some criminal activities by "former, frustrated combatants in certain parts of Nepal."29 [Citations omitted]

The RAD finds that many of these splinter groups have broken away from the central "Maoist" identity and values. The RAD notes, as discussed previously, that all of the Appellants' problems with the Maoists occurred in their home area with a separatist Maoist faction (a splinter group) described as the Biplav faction (Netra Bikram Chand Biplav).30

The documentary evidence indicates that this group, composed of former, frustrated combatants and other factions that have rejected accommodation with the elected government,31 is involved in criminal activity and extortion. The documentary evidence further confirms that the Unified Communist Party or Nepal-Maoists that joined the peace process in April 2006 has since split into five groups, one of which is the dissident Biplav group. The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that the Biplav faction is a dissident group operating outside of the ruling government. They engage in extortion, mainly outside of Kathmandu in the Mid-West and Far-West regions of Nepal.32 The RAD has previously noted that there is evidence that indicates that the Biplav group has participated in activities designed to disrupt elections in Kathmandu. The evidence further confirms that the authorities have taken an aggressive stance in curtailing the groups' presence in Kathmandu.

The RAD finds that while a few articles indicate the Biplav Maoist groups may be involved in activities in the Kathmandu, the evidence does not indicate that they have been active in extortion and kidnapping of individuals with a profile similar to the Appellants in Kathmandu.

The RAD has reviewed the Appellants' testimony and statements in the record. The RAD finds the Appellants' problems, as described in their testimony, and the supporting documents submitted, all centred in their home area in XXXX, some 280 km from Kathmandu. The RAD notes the extortion demands were associated with a local Biplav Maoist group over a two month period beginning in February 2017. The Appellants left the area in April 2017 and stayed in Kathmandu for three months without any problems from the agent of persecution before they left for Canada. The Appellants submit that living safely for three months in Kathmandu does not confirm that the location is reasonable or safe. The RAD notes that the Appellants had at least five interactions with the local Maoists in a short period of time before they left for Kathmandu. The RAD finds it reasonable to believe that if this group was persistent in its extortion and pursuit of the Appellants, and if they had the ability, they would have discovered the Appellants in Kathmandu. The RAD further notes that the Appellants two children have remained with their grandparents in Kathmandu without any reported problems. The Ability of the Agent of Persecution to Communicate Throughout Nepal

The RAD has considered if the Appellants will face risk in relocating to Kathmandu due to their profile as individuals who were being sought for extortion by their local Biplav Maoist group. The RPD found that the objective evidence provides limited support for the Appellants' assertion that the Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout the country; and, found little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the larger Maoist network. The Appellants submit that the evidence confirms the Maoists have a nationwide network, giving them the ability to find them anywhere in Nepal. The Appellants further submit that the RPD as well as the documentary evidence confirm this fact. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellants.

The RAD notes the principal Appellant was asked how he knew that the Maoists network would be able to able to find him and his wife. He answered that maybe they would use their telephones to call local cadres and find them. The RAD finds the principal Appellant's explanation provides little support for his allegations as to the Maoist's communication ability, and that this explanation amounts to simple speculation.

The RAD has reviewed the documentary evidence before the RPD, which includes both the IRB's National Documentation Package (NDP) and the Appellants' documentary evidence. The RAD finds that the IRB's objective evidence makes a statement that the Young Communist League (YCL), a youth offshoot of the Maoist party, has a "nationwide network,"33 but beyond that, the detailed information in this document addressing the actions of the YCL towards those associated with opposing political views provides no additional information about the ability of various divisions to communicate and share information throughout the country. The RAD further notes the documentary evidence does not confirm any linkage between the YCL and the Biplav Maoists. Nor does it make any mention of the ability of the numerous Maoist factions to communicate with each other or whether they would have any interest in sharing information due to their opposing political viewpoints. The RAD's review of the documentary evidence finds little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the large number of Maoist groups and if/how the different regions coordinate and share information including in circumstances such as the Appellants'.

The RAD additionally notes that much of Nepal's communication infrastructure was destroyed in the 2015 earthquake. The country's telephone communication system is described as "poor," its mobile- cellular network is described as "fair," and internet penetration is 17.6 percent of the population.34 The RAD finds the documentary evidence confirms that communication is limited. The RAD finds the singular statement in the documentary evidence, as well as the Appellants' statements about the Maoist "network," are vague and non-specific and they are not supported by any additional evidence before the RAD.

The RAD finds on its review of all of the evidence, that there is insufficient persuasive evidence to support the Appellants' allegations that the local Biplav Maoists in their home area have an ability to communicate throughout Nepal in order to locate the Appellants. The RAD finds the Appellants' problems are limited and local to XXXX. The RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this issue and the Appellants' argument must fail.

The RAD notes that in order to target the Appellant in Kathmandu, the agent of persecution would be required to: 1) Learn the Appellants have returned to Nepal; 2) Learn the Appellants have relocated to Kathmandu; and, 3) Determine the whereabouts of the Appellants in Kathmandu.

The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that if an organization was of sufficient strength and reach to be able to learn of a person's return to Nepal, or their presence in any city in the country, there would be objective evidence to support this.

The RAD has reviewed the submissions of the Appellants and the available documentary evidence, and finds that as much as it accepts that the Appellants were targeted by local individuals whom they identified as members of the Biplav Maoists, there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellants' return to Nepal upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellants' movements within Nepal. Second Prong

The RPD found that when it considered the Appellants' particular circumstances, it was objectively reasonable for them to reside in Kathmandu. The principal Appellant stated that they would not have any problems if the Maoists were not targeting them. The RAD notes that the Appellants did not advance any additional testimony or provide reasons in their Memorandum as to why they would not be able to reside in the proposed IFA location. The RAD notes: * The Appellants both have twelve years of education, which includes 2 years of post-secondary schooling.35 * Both Appellants are fluent in the Nepali language as well as English. * The principal and associate Appellants have extensive work experience in the optical business.36 * The Appellants have friends and family members in Kathmandu who would likely be available to assist the Appellants in their relocation. * The Appellants provided testimony to indicate that they had relocated in Nepal on a previous occasion. * The Appellants are experienced international travellers. They have travelled to Canada and resettled without reporting any significant problems.

The RAD finds after a review of all of the evidence, that given the Appellants' personal circumstances, it is not unduly harsh or objectively unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Kathmandu in Nepal. Conclusions on IFA

Upon review of the record, including the testimony of the Appellants, their documentary evidence, and the information available in the NDP, the RAD agrees with the conclusion of the RPD for the same reasons37 - that Kathmandu offers the Appellants a viable IFA within Nepal; the claim therefore fails on this basis.

Once the IFA has been named, the burden is on the Appellants to show that either of the two prongs of the Rasaratnam test are not met. There is insufficient evidence in the record to suggest that the Biplav Maoists from their home region would have the reach or influence to locate the Appellants elsewhere in Nepal, including specifically in Kathmandu. The RAD further finds that they would not be able to enlist other Maoist factions to conduct a national search for the Appellants, such that it would give rise to a serious possibility of persecution or subject them personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. Likewise, they have not demonstrated that in their personal circumstances, the proposed IFA would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh. As noted above, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA to Kathmandu once raised, and the RAD finds that the Appellants have not discharged that burden.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
